title: Trintellix and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Vortioxetine?
excerpt: Can you drink on Trintellix? How vortioxetine and alcohol interact, why nausea and next-day mood get worse, which hangover medicines to avoid, and when to call a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Trintellix (vortioxetine)? What the label says about alcohol, side effects it worsens, hangover meds to avoid, and when to call a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most doctors and pharmacists will tell you to avoid alcohol, or at least keep it light, while you take Trintellix (vortioxetine). That advice isn't because the combination is acutely dangerous in the way alcohol plus opioids or sleeping pills can be. In a study described in the US prescribing information, a single dose of alcohol given alongside vortioxetine didn't change blood levels of either one and didn't make thinking and coordination meaningfully worse than alcohol alone. The real reasons for caution are slower and more personal: alcohol is a depressant that works against the very thing the medication is treating, it tends to make Trintellix's most common side effects (nausea and dizziness) feel worse, it disrupts sleep, and it can turn a normal hangover into a day of heavy anxiety and low mood.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink in the first few weeks of treatment or right after a dose change, until you know how the medication affects you. Don't skip doses to "make room" for drinking. Expect your old limit to be too much. Be careful with ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin for a hangover, and avoid cough syrups with dextromethorphan and any "serotonin" supplements unless your doctor has okayed them. If drinking leaves you feeling hopeless or having thoughts of hurting yourself, stop and get help right away.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor.** This article explains general research and the official label for vortioxetine. It isn't a substitute for the doctor who prescribed your medication, who knows why you take it, what dose you're on, and what else you take. **Talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before drinking on Trintellix if** you've just started or changed your dose, you take other medicines that affect serotonin or bleeding, you have liver problems, you're older or have been told your sodium runs low, or you've noticed that alcohol makes your mood worse. **Get help right away if** you have thoughts of suicide or self-harm (call or text **988** in the US), or you notice signs of serotonin syndrome such as agitation, fever, heavy sweating, a racing heart, muscle twitching or stiffness, or confusion. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Trintellix Is and How It Works

Trintellix is the brand name for **vortioxetine**, a prescription antidepressant approved in the US for major depressive disorder in adults. It was first sold under the name Brintellix and was renamed Trintellix in 2016 because the old name was being confused with Brilinta, an unrelated blood-thinning drug. So if you see "Brintellix and alcohol" online, it's the same medicine.

Vortioxetine is often described as "multimodal," which is a way of saying it does more than one thing at once. Like the familiar SSRIs (Lexapro, Zoloft, Prozac), it blocks the serotonin transporter, the pump that pulls serotonin back into nerve cells, so more serotonin stays active between them. On top of that, it acts directly on several individual serotonin receptors, switching some on and blocking others. That combination is thought to influence other brain chemicals indirectly, and it's one reason vortioxetine has been studied for the foggy thinking and slowed concentration that often come with depression.

A few practical facts matter for anyone thinking about alcohol:

- **It's taken once a day**, usually at 5, 10, 15, or 20 mg. Many people start at 10 mg and move up to 20 mg if they tolerate it.
- **It stays in your body a long time.** Vortioxetine has a half-life of roughly two and a half to three days, meaning it takes that long for the level in your blood to fall by half. It takes about two weeks to build up to a steady level.
- **It's cleared by the liver**, mainly through an enzyme called CYP2D6, and turned into inactive leftovers that leave in urine and stool.
- **It takes weeks to work.** Like other antidepressants, the full effect on mood often takes several weeks.

Those last three points come up again below, because they shape what drinking on Trintellix actually looks like.

## The Real Interaction: What Alcohol Does on Top of Vortioxetine

When people search "Trintellix and alcohol," they're usually asking one of two things: "Will this hurt me tonight?" and "Is this going to mess up my treatment?" The answers are different.

### Tonight: less of a chemical clash than you'd think

Vortioxetine and alcohol don't compete for the same main breakdown pathway in a way that's known to cause trouble. Alcohol is mostly processed by alcohol dehydrogenase and, in heavier drinkers, an enzyme called CYP2E1. Vortioxetine relies mainly on CYP2D6. The interaction study summarized in the prescribing information found no meaningful change in blood levels of either drug when they were taken together, and no significant extra impairment on tests of thinking and movement compared with alcohol alone.

That's reassuring, but it has limits. It was a controlled study with a measured, single dose of alcohol in healthy volunteers. It doesn't tell you how you'll feel after four drinks on an empty stomach, how the combination feels in someone with depression, or what happens with regular heavy drinking.

### Over time: working against your treatment

This is the more important part. Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. In the short term it can lift your mood and loosen anxiety, but as it wears off, many people feel lower, more anxious, and more irritable than before they started. Heavy or regular drinking is linked to worse depression and anxiety in general, and to poorer results from antidepressant treatment. Our guide on [alcohol and depression](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-depression) covers that two-way relationship in more detail.

On Trintellix, that pattern can show up as:

- **Mood dips the day after drinking**, sometimes out of proportion to how much you drank
- **Worse sleep**, which on its own can drag mood down for days
- **Harder-to-read progress.** If you're drinking regularly, it becomes difficult for you and your doctor to tell whether the medication is working, whether the dose is right, or whether alcohol is the thing holding you back

Alcohol also changes serotonin signaling for a few hours and then leaves it unsettled as it clears. If you're curious about the brain chemistry, see [alcohol and serotonin](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-serotonin). The short practical takeaway: an antidepressant is trying to steady a system that alcohol keeps nudging around.

## Side Effects That Alcohol Can Make Worse

Trintellix has a fairly distinctive side-effect profile, and several of its most common effects overlap with what alcohol does to you.

| Trintellix side effect | How alcohol can add to it |
|---|---|
| **Nausea** (the most common side effect, especially early and at higher doses) | Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and is a classic cause of next-day nausea and vomiting. Together they can make for a rough morning. |
| **Vomiting and constipation** | Drinking can cause vomiting and loose stools, and dehydration afterward can make constipation worse. |
| **Dizziness** | Alcohol affects balance and blood pressure. Stacking the two raises the chance of feeling unsteady or lightheaded. |
| **Unusual or vivid dreams, sleep changes** | Alcohol fragments sleep, especially in the second half of the night. |
| **Sexual side effects** (dose-related) | Alcohol can also lower arousal and performance, especially in larger amounts. |
| **Itching** (reported in a minority of people) | Alcohol widens blood vessels in the skin and can make flushing and itchiness more noticeable for some people. |

None of this is dangerous for most people, but it explains why many people on Trintellix find that drinking "doesn't agree with them" the way it used to. Nausea is the big one. If you're still in the early weeks and the nausea hasn't settled, adding alcohol is a reliable way to make it worse.

## Can You Drink on Trintellix at All?

There's no official "safe amount" of alcohol for people taking vortioxetine, and anyone who gives you a precise number is guessing. What you can say is that doctors tend to treat the question differently depending on where you are in treatment and how you drink.

**Situations where most doctors would say no alcohol:**

- The first few weeks after starting Trintellix
- The week or two after a dose change
- Any time your mood is unstable, you're having thoughts of self-harm, or you've noticed drinking makes your symptoms worse
- If you have a history of drinking more than you meant to, or using alcohol to cope with low mood

**Situations where some doctors are comfortable with occasional light drinking:**

- You've been on a stable dose for a while and feel well
- You've noticed no worsening of mood or side effects with a single drink
- You're not taking other medicines that add risk (see the next sections)

If you're in the second group and your doctor agrees, a sensible approach is to treat your tolerance as unknown. Let your prescriber set the amount, have it with food, and see how you feel that night and the next day. Some people find that a drink or two hits harder than it used to, mostly in the form of dizziness, sleepiness, or nausea, even though the lab study didn't show extra impairment.

### Is it safe to have one drink on Trintellix?

For many people who are stable on the medication, a single drink is unlikely to cause harm, and the label's interaction study supports that. But "unlikely to cause harm" isn't the same as "recommended." The best person to answer this for you is your prescriber, because the answer depends on why you take Trintellix, how well it's working, and your history with alcohol.

## Should You Skip a Dose So You Can Drink?

No. This is one of the most common mistakes people make with antidepressants, and it doesn't work the way people hope.

Because vortioxetine has such a long half-life, skipping one dose barely lowers the amount in your body. You wouldn't be "clearing it out" before a night out. You'd just be adding risk of uneven levels and, over time, worse control of your symptoms. Missing doses repeatedly can also bring on discontinuation symptoms. The prescribing information notes that some people stopping 15 or 20 mg abruptly in trials had temporary symptoms like headache and muscle tension, and it recommends stepping down to 10 mg for a week before stopping completely.

The long half-life is also why alcohol and Trintellix are never really "separated" by timing. Waiting a few hours between your pill and a drink doesn't change much, because the medication is in your system around the clock. If you take Trintellix, you're always drinking "on" it.

If you'd like to drink less often, the right move is to change how you drink, not how you take your medication. And if you're thinking about stopping Trintellix altogether, do it with your doctor so you can taper and watch for a return of symptoms.

## Trintellix and Hangovers: Why the Next Day Feels Worse

People on antidepressants often say their hangovers are worse than they used to be. With Trintellix, a few things tend to stack up:

- **Nausea on nausea.** If the medication already makes your stomach a bit unsettled, alcohol's effect on the stomach lining and the toxic by-product acetaldehyde can make the morning after genuinely miserable.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol may knock you out, but it breaks up sleep later in the night. Combined with the vivid dreams some people get on vortioxetine, you can wake up feeling like you barely slept.
- **"Hangxiety" and low mood.** The anxious, guilty, low feeling many people get the day after drinking can hit harder when you're being treated for depression or anxiety. It's usually temporary, but it's worth taking seriously. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why it happens and what helps.
- **Dehydration.** Alcohol makes you pee more, and dehydration adds to headache, dizziness, and fatigue.

What helps is mostly basic: eat before and while you drink, alternate with water, stop earlier than you used to, and give yourself an easy morning. For a broader plan, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

If the day after drinking regularly leaves you feeling much worse emotionally, tell your doctor. That's useful information about how alcohol and your treatment interact for you specifically.

## Hangover Medicines and Trintellix: What to Watch

The morning-after medicine cabinet is where many of the real interaction risks hide.

### Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin

Drugs that affect serotonin, including vortioxetine, can make bleeding more likely, because platelets (the cells that help blood clot) rely on serotonin to work properly. The Trintellix label warns that this risk goes up when it's combined with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen, aspirin, and blood thinners like warfarin. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining too, and NSAID labels already carry a stomach-bleeding warning for people who have 3 or more drinks a day.

One standard dose of ibuprofen taken with food is not usually a crisis for a healthy person, but regular use, high doses, or combining these factors raises the risk of stomach bleeding. Watch for black or tarry stools, vomit that looks like coffee grounds, or unusual bruising, and get care if you see them. Our [aspirin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) covers the stomach side of this in more detail. If you need a painkiller and have no liver concerns, ask a pharmacist whether a normal dose of acetaminophen is a better fit for you.

### Cough and cold products, migraine pills, and opioids

Serotonin syndrome is a rare but serious reaction caused by too much serotonin activity. Alcohol itself isn't a common trigger, but some things people take while drinking or hungover are. On top of Trintellix, be careful with:

- **Dextromethorphan**, the "DM" in many cough syrups and cold medicines
- **Triptans** for migraine, such as sumatriptan (often still used together under a doctor's supervision, but worth mentioning)
- **Tramadol** and some other opioid pain medicines
- **Other antidepressants**, St. John's wort, and supplements like 5-HTP or tryptophan
- **Recreational drugs** such as MDMA

Signs of serotonin syndrome include agitation or restlessness, confusion, a fast heartbeat, high blood pressure, fever, heavy sweating, shivering, muscle twitching or rigidity, and diarrhea. It can come on within hours of a new medicine or dose change. **This is an emergency. Call 911 or go to the ER.**

If you've seen 5-HTP sold as a "hangover mood" fix, read our [5-HTP and alcohol](/never-hungover/5-htp-and-alcohol) piece first. It's a supplement that directly raises serotonin, which is exactly what you don't want to stack on an antidepressant without medical advice.

### Medicines that change Trintellix levels

This one isn't about alcohol, but it often comes up in the same conversations. Strong CYP2D6 blockers can raise vortioxetine levels, and the label advises cutting the Trintellix dose in half when they're added. That list includes **bupropion** (Wellbutrin), fluoxetine (Prozac), paroxetine (Paxil), and quinidine. If you take Wellbutrin as well, it's worth knowing it has its own alcohol concerns, mainly a lower seizure threshold. See our [Wellbutrin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/wellbutrin-and-alcohol).

Strong enzyme inducers like rifampin, carbamazepine, and phenytoin do the opposite and can lower vortioxetine levels. Your doctor and pharmacist should already have these on their radar, but it's always worth mentioning any new prescription.

## Less Common Risks Worth Knowing

### Low sodium

Medicines that work on serotonin can occasionally cause low blood sodium (hyponatremia), especially in older adults and people taking diuretics. Drinking large amounts of low-sodium fluid, which can happen with heavy beer drinking over time, can also lower sodium. Symptoms include headache, confusion, weakness, unsteadiness, and in serious cases seizures. If you're older, on a water pill, or have had low sodium before, ask your doctor whether drinking is a good idea for you.

### Mood swings and mania

Antidepressants can trigger mania or hypomania in people with undiagnosed or known bipolar disorder. Alcohol can blur these signs. If you notice racing thoughts, very little need for sleep, unusually risky behavior, or a mood that feels "too high," tell your doctor.

### Suicidal thoughts

Like all antidepressants, Trintellix carries a boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behaviors in children, teenagers, and young adults under 25, particularly early in treatment and after dose changes. Alcohol lowers inhibition and can intensify low moods. If you ever feel hopeless or have thoughts of self-harm after drinking, stop drinking and reach out right away: call or text **988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US), contact your doctor, or go to the nearest emergency room.

## Vortioxetine Compared With Other Antidepressants and Alcohol

People often want to know whether Trintellix is "better" or "worse" with alcohol than other options. There isn't a good head-to-head study comparing alcohol effects across antidepressants, so be wary of anyone who ranks them confidently. A few general points are fair to make:

- **Compared with SSRIs like Lexapro and Zoloft:** the alcohol advice is very similar. The bigger differences are in side effects. Vortioxetine tends to cause more nausea and is often described as less sedating and less likely to cause weight gain. Our [Lexapro and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol) walks through that medicine's label.
- **Compared with more sedating antidepressants:** medicines like mirtazapine or trazodone add drowsiness, which alcohol amplifies. Vortioxetine is generally not as sedating, but that doesn't mean alcohol won't make you sleepy or unsteady.
- **Compared with bupropion:** Wellbutrin's main alcohol concern is seizures, which isn't a major issue with vortioxetine.

For a side-by-side overview of the main antidepressant classes, see our [antidepressants and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol).

## Practical Tips If You and Your Doctor Agree You Can Drink

If you've had the conversation and you're going to drink occasionally, these steps lower the odds of a bad night or a bad week:

1. **Keep taking your medication as prescribed.** Same time, same dose, no skipping.
2. **Know your limit before you start**, and make it the one your prescriber gave you, not your pre-medication habit.
3. **Eat a real meal first.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps with nausea.
4. **Alternate with water** and finish the night with a glass or two.
5. **Avoid mixing with sleep aids, cannabis, or other sedatives.**
6. **Skip hangover "stacks" with 5-HTP, St. John's wort, or SAMe.**
7. **Be thoughtful about the morning after.** Food, water, rest, and a careful choice of painkiller.
8. **Notice your mood for a day or two afterward.** If drinking reliably makes you feel worse, that's a signal worth acting on and sharing with your doctor.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

Some people look into supplements to soften hangovers, and DHM (dihydromyricetin) comes up often. Here's an honest view.

DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*). Lab and animal research suggests it may support the enzymes that break down alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, the same receptor family alcohol affects. Human research is limited. A small 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease reported improvements in some liver markers, but that isn't a hangover study. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it doesn't make it safer to drink on an antidepressant.

There also aren't any published studies on DHM taken together with vortioxetine. Because DHM affects brain signaling, the cautious move is to **ask your prescriber or pharmacist before adding it**, just as you would with any supplement while on Trintellix. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM with common medicines.

If your doctor is comfortable with it, commonly used options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). The [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Whatever you take, it doesn't replace the basics: drinking less, eating, and hydrating.

## The Bottom Line

- Trintellix (vortioxetine) and alcohol don't have a dramatic chemical clash. In the label's interaction study, a single dose of alcohol didn't change drug levels or add meaningful impairment.
- Most doctors still advise avoiding or limiting alcohol, because it works against depression treatment, worsens nausea, dizziness, and sleep, and can make next-day mood much worse.
- Don't drink in the first few weeks or after a dose change, and never skip doses to drink. The long half-life means skipping doesn't help anyway.
- Be careful with NSAIDs and aspirin for hangovers because of bleeding risk, and avoid dextromethorphan, 5-HTP, St. John's wort, and other serotonin boosters unless your doctor approves.
- Seek emergency care for signs of serotonin syndrome, and call or text 988 if you have thoughts of self-harm.
- The best answer for you comes from your prescriber, who knows your full history.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Trintellix?**

Most doctors advise avoiding alcohol or keeping it to occasional light drinking once you're stable on the medication. The prescribing information describes a study where a single dose of alcohol with vortioxetine didn't change drug levels or add meaningful impairment, but alcohol can still worsen depression, sleep, and side effects like nausea and dizziness. Ask your prescriber what makes sense for you.

**Does alcohol make Trintellix less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't appear to lower vortioxetine levels in the blood, but regular or heavy drinking can work against depression treatment. Alcohol is a depressant, disrupts sleep, and tends to worsen mood and anxiety as it wears off. That can make it harder for the medication to help and harder for you and your doctor to judge whether it's working.

**How long after taking Trintellix can I drink?**

Timing doesn't really separate the two. Vortioxetine has a half-life of roughly two and a half to three days, so it's in your system around the clock once you take it daily. Waiting a few hours after your dose won't change much. The more useful questions are how much you drink, whether you're stable on your dose, and whether your doctor is comfortable with it.

**Should I skip my Trintellix dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping a dose barely lowers the amount of vortioxetine in your body because of its long half-life, and repeated missed doses can make your symptoms harder to control or bring on discontinuation effects like headache and muscle tension. Keep taking it as prescribed and change how you drink instead.

**Why do I feel sick after drinking on Trintellix?**

Nausea is the most common side effect of vortioxetine, especially in the early weeks and at higher doses. Alcohol irritates the stomach and produces acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product that contributes to hangover nausea. The two together can make you feel much sicker than you would from either alone. Eating first, drinking less, and waiting until the early nausea settles can help.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover while on Trintellix?**

Use caution. Vortioxetine can raise bleeding risk, and the label warns that this risk goes up with NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen, aspirin, and blood thinners. Alcohol also irritates the stomach lining. An occasional standard dose with food may be fine for some people, but ask a pharmacist which pain reliever suits you, and get care for black stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.

**Is vortioxetine the same as Brintellix?**

Yes. Brintellix was the original US brand name for vortioxetine. It was renamed Trintellix in 2016 to avoid confusion with Brilinta, an unrelated heart medication. The alcohol guidance is the same for both names.

**Is it safe to take DHM with Trintellix?**

There are no published studies on DHM taken with vortioxetine. DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in the brain, so it's sensible to ask your prescriber or pharmacist before combining them. DHM doesn't make drinking on an antidepressant safer, and there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone.
